pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B8.1.4)
- B8.1.4.1 — Demonstrate an understanding of ratio, rate and proportions and use these to solve real-world mathematical problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- use ratio reasoning (conversion factors) to convert units of measurement
- solve unit rate problems, including unit pricing and constant speed
- draw and interpret travel (distance–time) graphs
- decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship using tables and graphs
- identify the constant of proportionality in tables, graphs, equations and descriptions

pages.title: Converting units with ratios
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.4.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Conversion factor** — Since 1 m = 100 cm, the ratios [[1 m/100 cm]] and [[100 cm/1 m]] are both equal to 1. Multiplying a measurement by such a ratio changes its unit but not its size. Choose the ratio whose **unwanted unit cancels**.
## ✏️ Example 4.1
Convert: a) 3.5 m to cm b) 4,250 m to km c) 750 ml to litres d) 72 km/h to m/s
**Solution**
a) 3.5 m × [[100 cm/1 m]] = **350 cm**
b) 4,250 m × [[1 km/1000 m]] = **4.25 km**
c) 750 ml × [[1 l/1000 ml]] = **0.75 l**
d) [[72 km/1 h]] × [[1000 m/1 km]] × [[1 h/3600 s]] = [[72000/3600]] m/s = **20 m/s**
## ✏️ Example 4.2
Agbo walks 4 km to school in 60 minutes. Rukiya walks 4,200 m in 45 minutes. Which learner is faster?
**Solution**
Use the same units: Agbo: 4,000 m ÷ 60 min ≈ **66.7 m/min**. Rukiya: 4,200 m ÷ 45 min ≈ **93.3 m/min**.
**Rukiya is faster.**

pages.title: Unit rates, unit prices and speed
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.4.1.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Unit rate** — A **unit rate** is a rate in which the second quantity is **1**, e.g. 252 calories per hour, GH₵6.50 per kg, 60 km per hour. Find it by dividing both terms of the ratio by the second term.
## ✏️ Example 4.3
Salamatu burns 756 calories in 3 hours of drumming, at a steady rate. How many calories does she burn per hour?
**Solution**
| **Calories burned** | **756** | **252** |
|---|---|---|
| Hours | 3 | 1 |
Divide both terms by 3: 756 ÷ 3 = 252. Salamatu burns **252 calories per hour**.
## ✏️ Example 4.4
It takes 7 hours to mow 4 lawns. At that rate, how many lawns can be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate are lawns being mowed?
**Solution**
35 hours = 5 × 7 hours, so the number of lawns = 5 × 4 = **20 lawns**.
Rate = [[4/7]] lawn per hour (≈ 0.57 lawns per hour), or [[7/4]] = 1.75 hours per lawn.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Speed** — **Speed =** [[distance/time]], so distance = speed × time and time = [[distance/speed]].
## ✏️ Example 4.5
A bus travels 180 km in 2 h 30 min. Find its average speed. How long will it take to travel 252 km at the same speed?
**Solution**
Speed = 180 ÷ 2.5 = **72 km/h**; time = 252 ÷ 72 = 3.5 h = **3 h 30 min**

pages.title: Travel graphs
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply the knowledge of speed to draw and interpret travel graphs (distance–time graphs).
Curriculum indicator B8.1.4.1.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Distance–time graph** — Time is on the horizontal axis and distance (from the starting point) on the vertical axis. A **sloping** line shows movement — the steeper the line, the greater the speed. A **horizontal** line shows the object is **stopped**. A line sloping **down** shows the return journey.
## ✏️ Example 4.6
A trader travels by car from Buduata to Adawso, 20 miles apart. After 60 minutes he stops at Assin, 8 miles from Buduata. 36 minutes later he continues to Adawso, arriving 24 minutes later. After resting for 12 minutes, he returns to Buduata in 48 minutes. Draw the travel graph and find the speed on each stage.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f09]]
Figure 4.1: Travel graph of the trader's journey
| **Stage** | **Time (min)** | **Distance (miles)** | **Speed** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buduata → Assin | 0 – 60 | 8 | 8 ÷ 1 h = **8 mph** |
| Stop at Assin | 60 – 96 | 0 | 0 |
| Assin → Adawso | 96 – 120 | 12 | 12 ÷ 0.4 h = **30 mph** |
| Rest at Adawso | 120 – 132 | 0 | 0 |
| Adawso → Buduata | 132 – 180 | 20 | 20 ÷ 0.8 h = **25 mph** |
The steepest part of the graph (Assin to Adawso) shows the fastest stage. The whole trip took 3 hours.

pages.title: Example 4.7
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 4.7
Interpret the travel graph of Kwame's cycle ride.
[[fig:m8-f10]]
Figure 4.2: Kwame's cycle ride
a) How far did he travel in the first hour? b) How long did he rest? c) Find his speed on the return journey. d) What was his average speed for the whole trip (including the rest)?
**Solution**
a) **15 km** b) From 1 h to 1.5 h: **30 minutes** c) He returned 25 km in 1 h (2.5 h to 3.5 h): **25 km/h**
d) Total distance 50 km in 3.5 h: 50 ÷ 3.5 ≈ **14.3 km/h**

pages.title: Proportional relationships
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Recognise and represent proportional relationships between quantities; decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.4.1.4
> 🔑 **Key idea: Proportional relationship** — Two quantities x and y are **proportional** if [[y/x]] is the same for every pair of values. The graph of a proportional relationship is a **straight line through the origin**.
## ✏️ Example 4.8
Decide whether each table shows a proportional relationship.
| **Table A: Pens (x)** | **2** | **4** | **6** | **8** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost GH₵ (y) | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
| **Table B: Hours (x)** | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Charge GH₵ (y) | 30 | 50 | 70 | 90 |
**Solution**
Table A: [[y/x]] = [[5/2]] = [[10/4]] = [[15/6]] = [[20/8]] = 2.5 for every pair → **proportional**.
Table B: [[30/1]] = 30, [[50/2]] = 25, … the ratios differ → **not proportional** (there is a fixed charge of GH₵10 plus GH₵20 per hour).
[[fig:m8-f11]]
Figure 4.3: A proportional graph passes through the origin; a non-proportional straight line does not

pages.title: The constant of proportionality
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.4.1.5
> 🔑 **Key idea: Constant of proportionality** — If y is proportional to x then **y = kx**, where **k =** [[y/x]] is the **constant of proportionality**. It is the unit rate — the value of y when x = 1 — and the steepness of the graph.
## ✏️ Example 4.9
Identify the constant of proportionality: a) in Table A of Example 4.8 b) in the equation C = 12.5n for the cost of n bags of sachet water c) from the graph through (0, 0) and (4, 10).
**Solution**
a) **k = 2.5** (GH₵2.50 per pen) b) **k = 12.5** (GH₵12.50 per bag) c) k = [[10/4]] = **2.5**
## ✏️ Example 4.10
An ant travels [[9/8]] inches in 45 seconds and [[27/8]] inches in 2 minutes 15 seconds. Is its motion proportional? What is the constant of proportionality?
**Solution**
2 min 15 s = 135 s.
9/8/45 = [[9/360]] = [[1/40]] and 27/8/135 = [[27/1080]] = [[1/40]]
The ratios are equal, so the motion is proportional with **k =** [[1/40]] **inch per second** (0.025 in/s): d = [[1/40]]t.

pages.title: Chapter 4 summary
pages.body:
- Use conversion factors (ratios equal to 1) to change units.
- Unit rate: amount per one unit. Speed = distance ÷ time.
- On a travel graph, slope = speed; flat = stopped.
- Proportional: y = kx, a straight-line graph through the origin; k = [[y/x]] is the constant of proportionality.
